Full blog post, around my usual length (~1200 words). Core question: if AI writes more code, is it still worth becoming an engineer? My answer is yes. I don't necessarily expect more engineers overall, but people who can build high-quality systems for real needs can still be extremely valuable.

Use this as a loose thought dump. Decide the structure, ordering, headings, transitions, and emphasis yourself rather than treating each group of notes as a required section.

- Jevons paradox: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox. Better steam engines made power cheaper, which led factories to burn more coal rather than less. If coding gets dramatically cheaper, we probably get much more software: household-specific apps, heavily customized internal tools, and products for smaller needs. Not all of it requires professional engineers, but a much larger market still needs people who can manage and harden important systems.
- Efficiency can broaden both access and the spread between cheap and premium. Fashion moved from owning a few pieces to full closets, while handmade suits, $200 merino shirts, and $5,000 jackets still exist. Air travel ranges from basic economy to first-class suites and private jets. Software may become similarly bimodal: abundant cheap software plus a higher high end for scale, reliability, and difficult tradeoffs.
- Engineers may spend less time directly implementing and more time orchestrating. Pilots on long flights rely heavily on autopilot while handling air-traffic communication, weather, routing, and contingencies: https://simpleflying.com/what-pilots-actually-do-14-hour-flight-autopilot-handleing-everything/. Engineering could shift toward requirements, design, supervising implementation, testing, rollout, maintenance, and customer understanding.
- A related shift already happened from operations to DevOps and production engineering. Use the Cursor conversation with Simon Eskildsen as context: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bWyOyyrVIXk. The role expanded from SSH and configuration into code, Kubernetes, Terraform, cloud infrastructure, observability, and logging. Fewer specialists may be needed, but the strongest ones become more valuable. Generalist engineering may similarly blend with product and design without implementation skill disappearing entirely.
- The future has an appealing side: more custom software, better access to health information, personalized diagnoses, and easier communication across languages.
- It also has an ugly side: more stratification and a higher Gini coefficient. Scarce positional goods such as desirable housing and top education do not automatically get cheaper when software does; concentrated wealth may make them harder to reach.

Land wherever the argument naturally leads. Keep the outlook mixed rather than purely optimistic or pessimistic, and avoid promotional language.

blog post: "five opinions on building things well". full post. these used to live on a standalone opinions page on the site - first four are from oct 2023, fifth added nov 2025. open with a self-deprecating note (who cares about my opinions) but a similar opinions section in college started good conversations so maybe again.

# stay long enough to live with your own decisions
- engineers mostly hop jobs; the best ones i know stay a long time. hard watching peers go to flashy places w big salaries/titles but staying = deep wisdom + perspective
- caveat: needs to be a good company (growing, trust leadership). then:
 - you learn how your decisions turned out. feedback cycle. leave too soon and you never see if what you built was good or bad
 - you evolve as the company changes, get opportunities you wouldnt get as a new hire elsewhere
 - confidence in making things happen, you learn what it takes to ship there

# creativity should go to the right place
- antique tables still around from hundreds of years ago -> mortise and tenon. simple, strong, gold standard for thousands of years
- but STYLE varies wildly: ornate federal w marquetry/inlays (1700s) vs big craftsman pieces (early 1900s)
- software: build the bones in a standard way (battle tested tooling, postgres), spend creativity on solving user problems in the product

# not "speed vs quality", "speed + quality"
- biggest determinant of quality = skill of the craftsperson, not time spent on quality. on the margin more time helps, but a skilled person making a table is faster AND better than an unskilled person focusing hard on quality
- so talk about speed + quality: get more skilled so you finish faster with higher quality
- example: frank strazza http://www.strazzafurniture.com/ master woodworker, dovetail demo at texas woodworking festival https://texaswoodworkingfestival.com/, half blind dovetails in 15 min, way cleaner than an amateur taking an hour+
- all disciplines: amateur cant make high quality yet; experience -> better methods/tools/knowledge -> faster, and your minimum bar rises
- software: russ cox pdf library https://github.com/rsc/pdf, wrote it over a few weekends bc he needed to parse pdfs, still used everywhere incl assembled, one of the main go pdf libs
- takeaway: build lots of stuff, keep improving, seek feedback

# beta fast, launch slow
- stripe https://www.stripe.com mantra: beta users at 25%, launch at 98%. validate product/idea early w real users, but super high bar for public launch (all kinks out)
- we use the same at assembled

# taking meaningful risks sometimes means making people unhappy
- doing anything meaningful -> someone annoyed/uncomfortable/mad eventually. nobody ever upset = maybe avoiding hard conversations, tradeoffs, ambitious bets
- when someone's mad, two questions: mad at a specific action i took (careless, unfair, no context)? or mad at what i represent (direction change, a standard, breaking status quo)?
- actions -> fix/apologize/do better. what i represent -> usually a kernel of truth but doesnt mean back down

short blog post, explainer. mamba-3 dropped yesterday. big milestone vs the transformer stranglehold.

- state space model, a different architecture from transformers. current frontier systems such as gemini 3, opus 4.6, and gpt 5.4 still use transformers
- transformers: KV cache = huge memory of everything said so far, used when computing next token. needed bc looking at history is core to reasoning over lots of input (self attention)
- downside: more inputs (prefill, reading your system prompt) and outputs (decoding) -> KV cache grows per token -> quadratic memory, big inputs slow it down. labs have clever fixes but base math still slows over time
- SSMs (mamba) keep ONE fixed size hidden state h that updates: $h_t = A_t \, h_{t-1} + B_t \, x_t$, A_t and B_t data dependent, generated from current input x_t. model selectively remembers/forgets

magical things:
1. linear in context not quadratic. perfect for audio (way more data than text). why cartesia leads audio, their lab pioneered modern SSMs
2. linear algebra trick for prefill: $h_1 = A_1 \, h_0 + B_1 \, x_1$, $h_2 = A_2 \, h_1 + B_2 \, x_2$ so you can skip computing h_1: $$h_2 = A_2 \, A_1 \, h_0 + A_2 \, B_1 \, x_1 + B_2 \, x_2$$ - used to have to compute each token and feed into the next, now jump to the last hidden state directly. then for decoding switch to one state at a time

mamba-3 specifically targets inference efficiency. team correctly sees the shift: coding models / LLMs running bigger workloads -> inference is a bigger share of GPU usage. used to be mostly research/training, now inference matters way more.
optimizations:
- multi-input multi-output: earlier mambas computed output tokens one at a time like transformers. GPUs bottlenecked on moving memory VRAM -> compute cores, so they grouped multiple state updates into one big matmul, more math per memory wait
- complex numbers for memory: real number multiplied repeatedly only goes up or down (0.9 -> 0, 1.1 -> infinity). old mamba memory = real numbers -> given enough time you definitely forget or definitely remember. complex numbers rotate: multiply 1 by i four times and you're back to 1 ($1 \cdot i = i$, $i \cdot i = -1$, ${-1} \cdot i = -i$, ${-i} \cdot i = 1$). so mamba-3 can track cycles / oscillations

close: big labs still mostly optimizing transformers, but hybrids exist (AI21 jamba, google griffin), bet the next wave is mamba blocks + transformer blocks combined, soon.

Personal essay about time and how much of it we have. The tension is that life can feel incredibly long or incredibly short depending on how you look at it. The coastline paradox is a useful image: the land is finite, but its measured edge grows toward infinity as you look more closely.

Use these as loose notes. Decide the structure, sequence, headings, transitions, and ending yourself.

- US life expectancy is much longer than a century ago: roughly 76 for men and 81 for women. Those figures are pulled down by COVID and overdoses, so a healthy person may have another five to ten years: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm
- I've watched people have major renaissances in their forties and fifties. They usually compound years of work rather than appearing from nowhere.
- Eric Yuan, Chip Wilson, Tony Fadell, and Joseph Lubin started their best-known companies after forty. Most unicorn founders are in their thirties (https://www.patreon.com/TheVentureMindset/shop/unicorn-report-466660?source=storefront), with average industry experience rising from eight years in 2010 to fourteen: https://www.signalfire.com/blog/unicorn-founder-origins-data-report
- Jensen Huang spent about thirty years building Nvidia before the LLM wave put it in exactly the right position. OpenAI had a shorter version of this arc; I remember OpenAI Five beating the Dota 2 champions when it still looked like an impressive toy: https://openai.com/index/openai-five-defeats-dota-2-world-champions/
- Subjective time speeds up with age: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16512313/. Daily life contains less novelty, and each year becomes a smaller fraction of everything already lived—one tenth of a ten-year-old's life but one fortieth of a forty-year-old's.
- Michel Siffre spent months in a cave without sunlight or clocks: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10115684/. He believed around 150 days had passed when it was closer to 180, and counting what felt like 120 seconds took about five minutes. Deep focus creates a gentler version of that compression.
- Energy and physical resilience also change. People in their forties and fifties warned me that injuries heal more slowly and tiredness hits harder. Now in my thirties, my mind still generates far more projects than I can pursue, while late nights and poor sleep take a noticeably larger toll.
- The long view means there is time for learning, building, and compounding. The short view means the high-energy, high-novelty years are finite and feel increasingly fast.
- Personally, I feel lucky to work on things I enjoy and learn from remarkable people. I also want to remember to pause and appreciate the experience while it is happening.

Blog post. Core opinion: token count should not be the primary north-star metric for an engineering team's AI adoption. It can be one useful measure, but gamifying it as the measure will create bad incentives.

Treat these as loose notes. Choose the structure, ordering, headings, and conclusion yourself.

- Token usage scales directly with cost. That may look harmless early, but usage becomes embedded in workflows and automations. Later, reducing a large Anthropic or OpenAI bill means tracing where tokens go, deciding which uses are worthwhile, and migrating systems people now depend on.
- A token target rewards consumption rather than good work. It creates “slop cannons”: people are encouraged to spend tokens and merge low-quality output. From the metric's point of view, burning a million tokens without solving the problem earns the same score as using them to finish a difficult refactor.
- I still want people using AI and changing how they work. The hard part is genuine behavior change, not setting a quota. Start with the curious people who already see the potential. Let them build visible things, share internal demos, tell concrete stories about work going from hours to minutes, and pair with people who have not had the same realization yet.
- If adoption is low, the problem is usually rough tooling, unclear workflows, or nobody demonstrating what good looks like. A token counter does not solve those problems.
- Look primarily at outputs: are engineers shipping more than six months ago, resolving customer problems faster, attempting projects they would previously avoid, and feeling energized rather than drained?
- Keep token data for cost forecasting, adoption trends, and identifying people who might benefit from coaching. Just do not confuse the input with the outcome.

blog post. "why are executives enamored with AI but ICs aren't?" the topic labels below organize the notes; choose the final structure and headings yourself.

- clear divide in AI perception: execs love it, evangelize, even mandate usage. ICs much more skeptical. shows up everywhere - HN threads, internal slack debates about coding agents
- my posit: execs have always dealt w non-determinism and design nondeterministic systems. ICs are evaluated on executing deterministic tasks

# managing non-deterministic systems
- execs always deal w non determinism, par for the course:
 - people out sick / unexpected time off
 - someone quietly misses an important deadline and only surfaces it after the damage is done
 - people reacting to an announcement unexpectedly
 - a feature built in a way that technically hits objectives but doesnt fit the rest of the product
- chaos theory class: nonlinear chaotic systems emerge when agents act w different inputs/utility functions. easier to manage if you make utility functions consistent (get a grasp on dynamics)
- manager's job = build a model of the world + align everyone's utility functions knowing there's lots of non-determinism. so managers are ok w a decent amount of it
- AI = non deterministic but behaves like a well behaved chaotic system (understand general behavior, cant predict specific outcomes). e.g.:
 - LLMs keep working and produce output regardless of time of day, difficulty, info available
 - failure modes are well defined (hallucinations, cant operate outside context, bad when underspecified)
 - task envelope is fairly well known and getting mapped fast. unlike humans where each person has different strengths you uncover over time
- many of these are MORE deterministic than large human systems -> super attractive to an exec who already invests in adding determinism (process, levels/ladders, SOPs)

# why individual-contributor work feels more deterministic
- ICs focus on specific problems w specific inputs/outcomes. correctness easier to determine. job quality ~ quality + speed w weights depending on org. changes as you go up (staff eng = ambiguous business problems) but most ICs = well defined world
- ICs do face non-determinism (unclear reqs, flaky systems, shifting priorities) but evaluation pushes the other way. value = reliably precise (correct code, right analysis, design that holds up). more deterministic output = better at your job
- AI injects non determinism exactly there. reasons to be skeptical:
 - **not as good as them at their job**: trained human on a specific task often beats an LLM, esp long running, multi system, precise domain intuition. expert handed a mediocre tool -> fixing its mistakes costs more than doing it yourself
 - **changes what the job is**: doing the work -> managing the thing that does the work. skills that got you hired (focus, precision, domain knowledge) arent the skills for that. disorienting
 - **tied to self worth**: work = majority of waking hours. execs say "AI makes everyone productive", ICs hear "the things you spent years on matter less". reasonable to feel regardless of what's said
- note: speed-biased orgs see more IC adoption (my startup eng network mostly adopting, speeding things up, not necessarily higher quality). quality-biased orgs see the opposite. AI doesnt really raise quality, hard to make it, sometimes lowers it on specific tasks bc these ICs are well trained for exactly that task

# where does the friction come from
- the day to day differs by layer of the org. execs manage nondeterministic systems, built careers on it. ICs in a deterministic world evaluated on precise reliable output. AI fits the first worldview neatly, the second awkwardly
- this explains a lot of the friction in broad AI rollouts. one tool, two completely different experiences, set by what your role demands

short punchy post (~250 words) for medium. "why blocking LLMs from your website is dumb"

- perplexity accused of scraping sites that blocked AI crawlers in robots.txt https://techcrunch.com/2025/08/04/perplexity-accused-of-scraping-websites-that-explicitly-blocked-ai-scraping/ -> wave of how-to guides for blocking LLM scrapers [footnote 0]. very vitriolic, moral angle ("AI is stealing your content") + general anti-AI distaste
- bold line: but how many of you wouldn't hook your site up to google?
- i put stuff online so someone else sees it. if i didnt want that id write in my notebook not the public web
- LLMs = next gen search layer. already generating massive pipeline for companies/sites that are good at getting their content shown in LLMs. plus most LLMs have agentic web search that actively produces links -> huge funnel of potential readers
- blocking feels righteous but walls you off from where distribution is growing fastest
- like any tech, use it right = lots of power, blocking it entirely = bad idea. upside to creators who adapt not hide
- close: high quality content that LLMs actually cite is the new game

medium post, ~700 words: product lessons from dan robinson (ex CTO of heap). recap of a dinner discussion.

- intro: at assembled https://www.assembled.com/ we try to have a culture of continuous learning, been inviting great startup people to share wisdom on building products. few weeks ago hosted dan robinson https://www.linkedin.com/in/dan-robinson-a6930726/ for dinner
- dan: one of the first engineers at heap https://www.heap.io/, CTO ~9 years, helped scale to 350+ employees and a $110M series D. seen scaling at many stages
- top takeaways as bullets:
 - execution execution execution: it mostly comes down to whether you build the thing users need
 - talk to users w intellectual honesty: careful w leading questions that bias users
 - taste the soup: use your own product as often as possible

# the burnt pizza problem
- pull quote from dan: you have to figure out whether the pizza is burnt (bad execution) or pizza was a bad idea
- default state of early startups = low inconsistent usage, so a key job is diagnosing low usage and finding ways to raise it
- burnt pizza framing: give test users burnt pizza, they dont like it - was pizza bad or was it just burnt? when heap shipped something w weak usage the question was: was the need wrong, or had the team executed poorly?
- interesting broader point: best companies often have ideas similar to tons of competitors. facebook/myspace/friendster very similar. facebook won on execution - viral features, moving fast, listening to users. didnt burn the pizza

# learning from users without biasing them
- YC says only two things: write code and talk to users https://www.ycombinator.com/library/4D-yc-s-essential-startup-advice. but hard to do it right without biasing them
- dan's story: a heap product that didnt work out. tons of internal meetings on how to build it + fit into strategy, THEN talked to customers. leads to questions like "if you had X would you use it" / "is X a good idea" -> users say nice things, no skin in the game, no info on real value
- next launch (much more successful): got precise about how to learn what users wanted. "how would you articulate the value to a teammate" (how they think about value), "what have you already done to solve this" (how real the problem is). asked pilot users to pay - the true test
- ultimately: intellectual honesty (bold). easy way to waste months on something nobody needs = letting your excitement distort the user conversations. be as unbiased as possible about the problems users actually face

long personal narrative for medium. possible title idea: the path from a failed YC company through early Stripe to eventually raising $20M

start w a bolded lessons list for people who dont want the rambling narrative:
- figure out what great looks like
- get lucky, then capitalize on it
- ok to miss your top choice, your optimization function may differ in a couple years
- hard to spot great businesses, easier to spot great people -> narrows the window
- failing gives better perspective than being told you'll fail
- great engineers arent defined by tenure. combine strong product judgment with enough technical skill to make the experience excellent
- early company decisions compound

surface the lessons as callouts where useful; decide their placement and how to group the narrative

# learning a quality bar through Rails contributions
- junior year MIT, open source class. favorite memory: open source conference, met aaron patterson / tenderlove https://github.com/tenderlove. rails core, fascinating person (see his site https://tenderlovemaking.com/). never seen anyone fix bugs that fast or know linux/rails/ruby that deeply. [photo caption: group photo w aaron at the conference]
- wanted to be as good as him -> started fixing small rails bugs. 6 months of extra hours before class (and during least favorite classes). sheer luck that my first professional dev experience was on one of the most influential web frameworks. core team held every PR to a high bar, learned a lot about good code
- (lesson: get lucky, capitalize) summer: first big project = major refactor of rails app structure. my patch https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/9655 hit lots of issues, never merged. learned big changes to heavily used code usually go badly esp when you dont understand the system
- persisted w smaller patches, climbed into top 50 contributors (still top 100 today https://contributors.rubyonrails.org/contributors/john-j-wang/commits). commits petered out as school + job hunt started

# looking for a job in silicon valley (lesson: ok to miss top choice)
- one company stood out: meteor https://www.meteor.com/. ex-asana team, open source framework pushing db changes to frontend. combined my love of open source + exciting new tech. didnt get the job
- devastated then, good thing in hindsight. offers from small to large cos, took a little known company called stripe
- stripe not obvious then: parents never heard of it, friends neither (years before they knew what stripe did). salary hard to square vs big tech money/stability. tried to negotiate but pay was standardized across engineers. i also still wanted open source work (still bummed about meteor)
- loved SV excitement, wanted a place to be a sponge. lots of exciting cos (big data from famous professors, next frontend framework). every startup seemed to be growing. external factors = lagging indicators of great companies
- (lesson: spot great people) stripe slightly different: intelligent people, humility + care. everyone cared about the job and about me, all high powered. in awe of nelson elhage https://nelhage.com/ and evan broder https://ebroder.net/about/ working on hot swapping a linux kernel w/o reboot. always excited to talk problems
- recruiting care: patrick collison https://patrickcollison.com/ coffee walk w me, everything from stripe trying to acquire a defunct bank to economic drivers of productivity. introduced me (random college kid) to investors. literally shaking when michael moritz https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moritz and paul graham http://www.paulgraham.com/ did 20 min chats w me
- thoughtfulness + drive set stripe apart. many cos had one, few had both

# starting a YC company
- about to start at stripe in summer, then max kolysh (now CEO of dover http://www.dover.com/) sat me down for chipotle lunch. november senior year, planned to spend last semester learning not caring about grades
- max + doug feigelson https://www.linkedin.com/in/doug-feigelson-95371825/ got into YC building an API to connect online shopping. idea seemed a bit ridiculous but max/doug were smart, driven, humble. i always optimize environment for learning + great people -> next thing i know im signing incorporation docs and flying to mountain view. no idea what id do about stripe come summer, figure it out later
- [photo captions: left - listening to PG talk before YC; middle - doug at his typical desk; right - max and doug talking to founders at YC mountain view office]
- duffel bag to palo alto to start zinc https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/zinc. learned to grind: wake ~noon, code till 8, quick dinner + gym, back at 11pm coding till 3-4am. people said too hard, i loved it, poured heart and soul in
- (lesson: failing > being told you'll fail) YC ended and we still had no real product. YC mentality = growth is paramount, did everything for growth -> consumer app losing money per transaction. YC = great forcing function for growth but we never figured out fundamentals. also learned 13 hrs/day of coding guarantees nothing
- hard lessons. shut down the product, startup experience ending, id already accepted stripe and was going to keep my word. june 2014 somber meeting w max and doug, went to stripe

# working at early stripe
- asked to delay start for family vacation, manager said start sooner take time later (stripe ~100 people, moving fast). artificial 1 month deadline to ship first project
- assigned improving email receipts w michelle bu https://www.linkedin.com/in/michellebu/. month of touching all parts of the infra, tons of code. night before launch stayed up all night polishing, slept in a phone booth, woke early to finish edits while michelle wrote the blog post
- (lesson: great engineers not defined by years) [photo caption: at an offsite working on stripe stuff]
- humble hardworking people. michelle was a codebase veteran, drove the project, wrote the launch post, and still put my name on it (post still up https://stripe.com/blog/improved-email-receipts). says a lot about her and stripe
- michelle taught me there are flavors of great engineer. some are oracles via knowledge/experience. she was 1 yr out of college and one of stripe's best (unsung hero type): high standards, proactively corrected problems, stayed close to customers, and shipped constantly

# building a profitable (mostly) bootstrapped business
- stripe doing incredibly well, electric atmosphere (ambition + humility). after 1.5 yrs i wanted something different. friends shocked when i joined stripe, equally shocked when i quit to go back to zinc. optimizing for learning, broader skills at a smaller co
- zinc found traction in a niche: before plaid https://plaid.com/ pioneered a similar model in finance, we built APIs into ecommerce sites for small businesses selling on amazon/ebay. within a couple years very profitable, millions/yr on ~$400k pre-seed. followed basecamp's lead: work life balance, small team, no VC
- (lesson: early decisions compound) loved zinc bc feedback loop was fast - see how decisions from months ago affect today. nodejs backend w callbacks haunted us for years, every change added cruft to a sprawling callback hierarchy. otoh devops investment let us cheaply scale thousands of servers across many cloud providers. every cent saved on servers = a dollar of profit

# carrying the accumulated lessons into assembled
- few years in, zinc in great shape but i itched for bigger problems. started talking to my brother ryan wang https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryanywang/ and old friend brian sze https://www.linkedin.com/in/briansze/, leading the internal tools team for stripe's support org
- stripe: even after years of triple-digit expansion, the company remained unusually serious about support. patrick used to invite engineers to his apartment to answer tickets. didnt scale, stripe relied on outdated tools to manage the support team. many companies had the same problems, support ecosystem lacked good tools
- vivid memory: first meeting w gofundme's support team, morgan wood https://www.linkedin.com/in/morgan-wood-gfm/ showed a google sheet w thousands of rows, color coded cells, multiple editors. while we were there someone made an accidental edit and the ops lead jordan philyaw https://www.linkedin.com/in/jordanphilyaw/ had to manually recreate the whole sheet. impressive wizardry, but tooling clearly needed to get better
- these struggles across the industry -> brian, ryan and i started assembled http://www.assembled.com/ to transform/elevate customer support. recently raised a $16M series A https://techcrunch.com/2021/03/12/assembled-an-operating-system-for-support-teams-raises-16-6m/, now applying the lessons to building a long lasting impactful company
- [photo captions: left - assembled's 2018 office aka my living room; right - first career fair where we couldnt even give away free pizza (recruiting is hard)]

medium post: "why support is the next payments". use the payments analogy throughout. the notes are grouped into four themes and include source quotes; decide the final organization and where the quotes work best.

intro
- when i left stripe to start a support company http://www.assembled.com/ people thought i was crazy, "why leave the rocket ship". but stripe taught me the long game, invest in opportunities nobody's looking at
- 2010: collisons saw a massive problem in an industry startups considered a backwater. everyone was on flashy consumer apps / social / buzzy tech, stripe stayed focused on the opportunity nobody saw
- i strongly believe a new wave of change is coming to support w many of the trappings of payments a decade ago. the two are analogous:

# a massive, growing market
- quote: bezos on proactively delighting customers earning trust and more business, long term view aligns customers + shareholders https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000119312513151836/d511111dex991.htm
- support = massive growing market + differentiator for the best businesses. like payments in 2010, macro factors converging:
 - **consumer expectations shifted**: amazon showed people great support (refunds for damaged items, tracking, missing items handled). people buy based on support quality. 2020 microsoft study https://clouddamcdnprodep.azureedge.net/gdc/gdcPiLLQw/original?ocid=mkto_eml_EM582302A1LA1 - 90% of consumers use support as a factor in whether to do business w a company. a decade ago barely a factor, now dominant
 - **world moving online**: covid accelerated it. online = 20%+ of retail now. best brands lead w online commerce - nike hit its 30% online goal ~3 yrs early https://fortune.com/2020/09/23/nike-q1-ecommerce-results-covid-19/
 - **companies have budget**: US has 2x as many support agents https://www.bls.gov/ooh/office-and-administrative-support/customer-service-representatives.htm as truck drivers https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes533032.htm. $105B market in US alone, lots of global spend in asia + south america. software market growing too - salesforce's service product now out-earns its namesake sales product https://www.saastr.com/5-interesting-learnings-from-salesforce-at-24b-arr/
- 2010 the world went digital and stripe rode the growth of internet businesses. today those businesses need superb support to compete

# complex, outdated tools and processes
- quote: patrick collison baffled at how convoluted/awkward online payments were, payment ecosystem felt hostile to people trying to build businesses online https://www.forbes.com/sites/roberthof/2015/08/18/in-conversation-stripe-ceo-patrick-collison-on-the-limitless-potential-of-payments/?sh=6beb2d85126a
- taking payments in 2010 was hard: walk into a bank, thousands in fees, arcane gateways, months. stripe fixed that
- scaling a support team today equally hard. zendesk/intercom send messages but dont manage the team - communication layer not intelligence layer. most businesses run a labyrinth of remote workers on spreadsheets, each w their own preferences/skills. many channels (chat, phone, twitter, whatsapp), timezones, specializations (developer questions at stripe vs refunding a transaction at gofundme)
- [image caption: actual industry leading support software, many still desktop based fighting to move to the cloud]
- most industry leading tools built for call centers = command and control worldview. manager hierarchy dictating efficiency, hyper specific requirements. depressing to visit a real call center: bathroom breaks scheduled in 3 min intervals, take too long -> lower score. software sold to fortune 500, millions/yr, team to implement/maintain. thats where todays support tooling came from
- quote: stewart butterfield on slack's value of looking out for each other, making everyone's lives a little simpler https://www.businessinsider.com/slack-ceo-stewart-butterfield-on-company-culture-he-admires-2015-7
- modern teams want to scale without a thousand-person call center. fast growing cos dont see agents as cogs, want systems rooted in empathetic support. new era of companies pushing this, old tools not ready

# fundamental infrastructure for the internet
- quote: patrick collison - google is a foundational component of the internet for information retrieval, there should be one for economic infrastructure, sorely lacking (same forbes link)
- payments + support both fundamental to running an online business, necessary and differentiating:
 - **foundational**: every online business must take payments and support customers. imagine buying online w no way to contact anyone about a lost package or defective product. like mailing a check for an online purchase - worked for 90s mail order catalogs, today having no support can kill an online business quickly
 - **shared infrastructure problem across industries**: same credit card network for everyone, not industry specific - balloon seller and enterprise software co use the same system. support the same across companies: glossier selling lipstick or monzo doing banking, you forecast incoming requests, route to the right people, solve fast and accurately. some requests longer/multi step, but right people right place right time is universal

# a hard, non-obvious problem
